reported_effect: Among participants achieving >=5% weight loss, 58% achieved NASH resolution and 82% achieved a 2-point reduction in NAS; greater weight loss was independently associated with greater histological improvement
study_design: Prospective lifestyle intervention with paired liver biopsies
limitations: Not randomized; weight loss was achieved through lifestyle intervention and the analysis is observational with respect to the amount of weight loss

reported_effect: All patients who lost 7-10% of body weight and had few risk factors had reduced NAS
study_design: Prospective lifestyle intervention with paired liver biopsies
limitations: Small subgroup and non-randomized intervention; the result is not a quantitative recipe-level effect

reported_effect: 90% of participants achieving >=10% weight loss had resolution of NASH
study_design: Prospective lifestyle intervention with paired liver biopsies

reported_effect: 45% of participants achieving >=10% weight loss had regression of fibrosis
study_design: Prospective lifestyle intervention with paired liver biopsies
limitations: Small subgroup; evidence is not sufficient to conclude that advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis is generally reversible through lifestyle weight loss

reported_effect: A meta-analysis of 10 RCTs reported statistically significant reductions in AST and GGT with Mediterranean diet interventions
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
limitations: The included interventions and populations were heterogeneous and pooled effects varied across outcomes
source: Sangouni et al., British Journal of Nutrition, 2022;128(7):1231-1239 (online 2021); DOI 10.1017/S0007114521002270; PMID 34165054

reported_effect: The meta-analysis found no statistically significant effect on ALT (WMD -0.55 IU/L; 95% CI -1.25 to 0.13)
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
limitations: Later evidence has reported a significant ALT reduction, so this finding should be interpreted as study-specific rather than as evidence of no effect overall
source: Sangouni et al., British Journal of Nutrition, 2022;128(7):1231-1239 (online 2021); DOI 10.1017/S0007114521002270; PMID 34165054

reported_effect: Mediterranean diet reduced ALT (MD -2.93 IU/L; 95% CI -5.68 to -0.19; 9 RCTs), liver stiffness (MD -0.35 kPa; 95% CI -0.54 to -0.16; 4 RCTs) and MRI-PDFF (MD -1.37%; 95% CI -2.33 to -0.40; 5 RCTs)
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
sample_size: 24 RCTs in the meta-analysis (2018-2024); 4-9 RCTs per outcome
limitations: The authors noted heterogeneity and called for larger, longer-term isocaloric RCTs with standardized outcome reporting
source: Stern et al., European Journal of Nutrition, 2026;65(2):58; DOI 10.1007/s00394-025-03870-z; PMID 41689666

intervention: Dietary interventions including Mediterranean diet and calorie restriction
outcome_measured: ALT, AST, FLI, hepatic steatosis and liver stiffness
reported_effect: A systematic review and meta-analysis found dietary interventions significantly improved ALT, AST, FLI, hepatic steatosis and liver stiffness
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and clinical controlled trials
limitations: Interventions and outcome assessment methods were heterogeneous and the evidence included both randomized and non-randomized controlled studies
source: Haigh et al., Clinical Nutrition, 2022; DOI 10.1016/j.clnu.2022.06.037; PMID 35947894

outcome_measured: ALT, hepatic steatosis and liver stiffness
reported_effect: The dietary-intervention meta-analysis reported favourable effects of calorie-restricted interventions on ALT, hepatic steatosis and liver stiffness
limitations: Calorie restriction was implemented through different dietary approaches and should not be interpreted as a fixed recipe-level dose-response
source: Haigh et al., Clinical Nutrition, 2022; DOI 10.1016/j.clnu.2022.06.037; PMID 35947894

reported_effect: A 2024 meta-analysis found no significant difference between Mediterranean and low-fat diets in improving liver enzymes, liver fat and related indices in the short term
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
limitations: This is a comparative finding and does not imply that either dietary pattern has no benefit compared with baseline
source: Xiong et al., Food & Function, 2024; PMID 39076035; DOI 10.1039/D4FO01461H

reported_effect: Exercise training increased the likelihood of achieving >=30% relative reduction in MRI-measured liver fat compared with control (OR 3.51; 95% CI 1.49-8.23)
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
limitations: MRI-measured liver fat is a non-invasive surrogate; exercise protocols varied across studies
source: Stine et al., American Journal of Gastroenterology, 2023; PMID 36705333; DOI 10.14309/ajg.0000000000002098

reported_effect: An exercise dose of >=750 MET-min/week was associated with greater treatment response; the odds of achieving >=30% relative reduction in MRI-measured liver fat were 3.73 (95% CI 1.34-10.41)
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
limitations: Dose categories were based on prescribed exercise volume and do not establish a food-level or recipe-level effect
source: Stine et al., American Journal of Gastroenterology, 2023; PMID 36705333; DOI 10.14309/ajg.0000000000002098

intervention: Improved diet quality similar to the Mediterranean dietary pattern; limiting ultra-processed foods and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages
outcome_measured: Histologically or non-invasively assessed liver injury
reported_effect: The 2024 EASL-EASD-EASO guideline recommends improving diet quality similar to the Mediterranean pattern, limiting ultra-processed foods rich in sugars and saturated fat, and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages
study_design: Clinical practice guideline based on evidence synthesis
limitations: Not a single intervention study and does not provide a quantitative recipe-level effect size
source: EASL-EASD-EASO Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of MASLD, Journal of Hepatology, 2024;81(3):492-542; DOI 10.1016/j.jhep.2024.04.031; PMID 38851997

reported_effect: The 2024 EASL-EASD-EASO guideline recommends physical activity and exercise to reduce steatosis, preferably >150 min/week of moderate or 75 min/week of vigorous-intensity activity
study_design: Clinical practice guideline based on evidence synthesis
limitations: Physical activity is not a food intervention; this row provides contextual evidence for the broader intervention layer
source: EASL-EASD-EASO Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of MASLD, Journal of Hepatology, 2024;81(3):492-542; DOI 10.1016/j.jhep.2024.04.031; PMID 38851997

intervention: Excess energy from saturated fat vs unsaturated fat vs simple sugars
reported_effect: Overfeeding 1,000 kcal/day for 3 weeks increased liver fat by 55% with saturated fat, 15% with unsaturated fat (P < 0.05 vs saturated) and 33% with simple sugars
effect_direction: Harmful (saturated fat > simple sugars > unsaturated fat)
limitations: Small, 3-week overfeeding trial; supports limiting saturated fat but does not give a recipe-level dose
source: Luukkonen et al., Diabetes Care, 2018;41(8):1732-1739; DOI 10.2337/dc18-0071; PMID 29844096

reported_effect: Hypercaloric fructose (+104-220 g/day) increased intrahepatocellular lipid (SMD 0.45; 95% CI 0.18-0.72) and ALT (MD 4.94 U/L; 95% CI 0.03-9.85)
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled feeding trials
sample_size: 6 hypercaloric trials (13 trials, 260 participants in total)
limitations: Few, small, short and low-quality trials at extreme doses; the authors attribute the effect mainly to excess energy
source: Chiu et al., European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2014;68(4):416-423; DOI 10.1038/ejcn.2014.8; PMID 24569542

intervention: Fructose exchanged isocalorically for other carbohydrates
reported_effect: No effect of fructose in isocaloric trials
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled feeding trials
sample_size: 7 isocaloric trials (13 trials, 260 participants in total)
limitations: Healthy participants and short trials; retained so that sugar is not treated as harmful independent of energy
source: Chiu et al., European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2014;68(4):416-423; DOI 10.1038/ejcn.2014.8; PMID 24569542
